signs.name: Figure of enfeeblement
signs.definition: The second sign of composition of the inversion-image (ASA becomes aSa): weak, aimless characters whose futile acts, shrunk to specks against the horizon, reveal an immense and indifferent world.
signs.deamer_quote: "weak characters reveal the sublime nature of the world" (p. 112)
deleuze_examples: Stroszek (Werner Herzog, 1977)
The Enigma of Kaspar Hauser (Werner Herzog, 1974) — the 'weaklings and idiots'
NOTE: Deamer's Section II gives no film examples; these are Deleuze's own Cinema 1 examples (not cited by Deamer) (C1: 185-186)

scenes: Three young men sit in silence at a round glass café table on a sunny square, a fountain jetting behind them; one checks his phone, one twirls a dead leaf, one yawns and stretches.
Characters wander Islamabad's streets alone or stare vacantly over the cityscape from the hills and tall buildings.
A ceiling fan overdubbed with helicopter sound: borrowed cinema standing in for experience.
On the way to the airport Hasan's car pulls level with an open-backed truck carrying an itinerant worker, and the class structure suddenly becomes visible to him.

signs.operation: Shrink the character in the frame and give them nothing to do, until the world around them becomes the event.
signs.shot_criteria: A small, idle or powerless figure visibly dwarfed by a large setting, or people shown doing nothing (sitting, waiting, drifting) while the environment dominates.
signs.gloss: weak characters reveal the sublime nature of the world
signs.question: Is the actor tiny compared with the world disclosed?

diff.difference: Do a weak character's small, futile acts make an immense, indifferent world swell into view (the tiny point fleeing to the horizon), rather than the world merely sitting there?
diff.axis: where the disproportion between action and situation lies: action outsizes a futile situation (sAs) → [futile action reveals an immense situation (aSa)] → sAs = aSa, trivial and immense indistinguishable

confusions.name: Quotidian
confusions.flip: It is Quotidian instead if the small acts are neither futile nor merely revelatory but carry their own petty heroism, so trivial and immense can't be separated.
confusions.why_not: Enfeeblement keeps the inversion one-way: the act is futile, the world is sublime.

confusions.name: Opsign
confusions.flip: It is an Opsign instead if the character no longer acts at all (a seer, not a weakling doing something) and the situation is a pure optical one cut from any sensory-motor response.
confusions.why_not: The enfeebled still acts, however feebly; the small form is inverted, not broken.

confusions.name: Any-space-whatever
confusions.flip: It is Any-space-whatever instead if the vast space is emptied or disconnected and carries affect in itself, with no character action measuring it.
confusions.why_not: Enfeeblement needs the weakling's act as the measure that reveals the grandiose; remove the act and it becomes affection.

diff.counterfeit: An establishing extreme long shot of a hiker on a ridge looks like enfeeblement but is just a perception/milieu shot unless the character's acts across the film are shown as futile against that world.

confidence.high: Recurrent futile, aimless acts by idiot/weakling figures staged against indifferent vastness (Stroszek, Kaspar Hauser).
confidence.medium: A slacker or drifter film where weakness is clear but the world is not made to swell.
confidence.low: One tiny-figure-in-landscape shot.

diff.deamer_anchor: "weak characters reveal the sublime nature of the world" (p. 112)

signs.name: Quotidian
signs.definition: Deamer's name for the unnamed genetic sign of inversion, where sublime and futile become 'the same thing': everyday situations and actions at once trivial and immense, the universe indifferent yet the only ground of action.
signs.deamer_quote: "the pettiness of our function is the heroism of life" (p. 113)
deleuze_examples: No film named: Deleuze only notes sublime and enfeebled can become 'the same thing' (C1: 186, via Deamer p. 110)

scenes: Sunlight spreads across bright white net curtains while Adam sits across a wooden desk from the new manager, who takes notes during his job interview.
A long night take of Adam on his motorbike, the headlight sweeping the white walls of an alleyway.
Adam at his window, sun on his bare torso, lets the curtain fall back to shut out his son being taken away for the army.
Adam and his wife feed each other watermelon while war footage plays on the TV; at the end dead leaves float on the abandoned hotel pool.

signs.operation: Hold a static medium shot on an ordinary gesture long enough for the world outside the frame to press in.
signs.shot_criteria: An ordinary, unremarkable daily activity or domestic/work space filmed plainly and patiently (curtains, desk, pool, meal, commute) with nothing dramatic happening in frame.
signs.gloss: everyday situations, everyday actions – sublime ↔ futile
signs.question: Has everyday life become both ridiculous and heroic?

diff.difference: Is an everyday act shown so that you cannot decide whether it is trivial or heroic, the situation both inconsequential and unfathomable at once?
diff.axis: where the disproportion between action and situation lies: action outsizes a futile situation (sAs) → futile action reveals an immense situation (aSa) → [sAs = aSa, trivial and immense indistinguishable]

confusions.name: Figure of enfeeblement
confusions.flip: It is Enfeeblement instead if the act reads plainly as futile and the world plainly as overwhelming.
confusions.why_not: In the quotidian the petty function is itself the heroism; neither pole dominates.

confusions.name: Opsign
confusions.flip: It is an Opsign instead if the everyday is shown as a pure optical situation where no one can act at all (Ozu's empty vase, still lifes) rather than as an act of duty.
confusions.why_not: The quotidian is still an action-figure: the character works, serves, carries on.

confusions.name: Body of attitude
confusions.flip: It is Body of attitude instead if the everyday is carried by the tired, waiting body whose postures express time, and action has dropped out.
confusions.why_not: The quotidian is about the ambivalent value of action, not the body's time.

diff.counterfeit: A montage of morning routines (coffee, commute) looks quotidian but is merely exposition unless the film makes the routine simultaneously petty and weighty.

confidence.high: Across a film, a duty-bound ordinary job is shown both as servility and as the only ground of valour (A Screaming Man).
confidence.medium: Everyday life is foregrounded but tilts clearly toward either sublime or futile.
confidence.low: Any single domestic or workplace shot.

diff.deamer_anchor: "the pettiness of our function is the heroism of life" (p. 113) - Deamer's naming

signs.name: Limit of the large form action-image
signs.definition: The first sign of composition of the discourse-image: the given milieu hides a question, and the character has to draw out that problem before any action can be a considered response rather than an explosive reaction.
signs.deamer_quote: "action explores a hidden problem" (p. 116)
deleuze_examples: Seven Samurai (Akira Kurosawa, 1954) — what is a samurai today?
Ikiru (Akira Kurosawa, 1952)
Dersu Uzala (Akira Kurosawa, 1975)
NOTE: Deamer's Section II gives no film examples; these are Deleuze's own Cinema 1 examples (not cited by Deamer) (C1: 188-190)

scenes: US and Mexican planes fly over the Infected Zone laying poison into the jungle below.
In the zone people smugglers have Scoot and Whitney sniff the air: the gas masks protect against the American chemicals, not the aliens.
A huge metal fence cuts across the continent and a concrete wall seals the US border; inside, towns are overgrown by jungle, and the pair come across an ancient Mayan temple.
At a deserted Texas gas station two luminous aliens twine their tentacles in the night sky, the creature's 'attack' revealed as a search for its mate, and the humans kiss.

signs.operation: Set up the fight, then turn the camera until the audience is no longer sure which side is the monster.
signs.shot_criteria: A situation built for conflict (wall, poison, masks, hunting, evacuation) whose image makes the aggressor/victim relation ambiguous or reversible; the frame raises a question instead of showing a duel.
signs.gloss: action explores a hidden problem
signs.question: What hidden question does this world contain?

diff.difference: Before acting, does the character have to extract a question hidden in the situation (what is a samurai now?), so action is delayed into a considered response rather than an explosive reaction?
diff.axis: where the problem is located: [a priori, hidden in the situation and extracted before a considered act] → a posteriori, actions assemble heterogeneous pieces that stay a cipher → everywhere, no originary form, the world itself a field of problems

confusions.name: Limit of the small form
confusions.flip: It is the Small-form limit instead if there is no given situation holding a question; the question is assembled from heterogeneous actions and stays unanswered.
confusions.why_not: In Ll the milieu is given and the question is a priori; a response is eventually possible.

confusions.name: Milieu
confusions.flip: It is Milieu instead if the situation simply provokes the character to a direct reply (SAS) with no pause to formulate its question.
confusions.why_not: Ll suspends the duel/response in favour of investigating the situation's givens.

confusions.name: Extreme limit
confusions.flip: It is the Extreme limit instead if you can't tell whether the problem came from the situation or from the actions, and the whole world has become a cipher of forces.
confusions.why_not: Ll still has a determinate milieu and a direction toward answer.

diff.counterfeit: A detective interrogating witnesses looks like a problem being extracted, but a whodunit's question is a missing fact, not a question hidden in the milieu that redefines what action can be.

confidence.high: The narrative visibly stalls action to investigate the givens and ends with an act framed as answer to the question (Seven Samurai, Ikiru).
confidence.medium: A questing structure where the question is posed but the response is conventional.
confidence.low: Any single shot; the sign is a narrative trajectory.

diff.deamer_anchor: "action explores a hidden problem" (p. 116)

signs.name: Limit of the small form action-image
signs.definition: The small form (action reveals situation) reflects on itself until action can no longer disclose the situation: parallel, heterogeneous lines of action connect only as a 'special homogeneity', leaving the question as a sustained, unanswered ellipsis.
signs.deamer_quote: the coordinates of a question will ultimately and necessarily be left unanswered (p. 117)
deleuze_examples: The Life of Oharu (Kenji Mizoguchi, 1952) - Deleuze's 'lines of the universe' passing through women (C1: 195)
Ugetsu (Kenji Mizoguchi, 1953)
signs.deleuze_examples_note: Deamer's Section II cites no films for this sign; examples are Deleuze's own (Cinema 1/2), supplied from knowledge of those books - verify before citing.

scenes: Three cops - Eddie, Tango, Sal - are intercut as three isolated lines that the film refuses to join.
Burned-out Eddie, a week from retirement, is saddled with a rookie ride-along whom he abandons.
The three protagonists fleetingly cross paths in one inner-city tower block, a crossing Deamer calls a ruse.
Their three outcomes read like three rolls of the dice, interchangeable between the men.

signs.operation: Cut parallel lines of action that never meet, and let the one moment they share space explain nothing.
signs.shot_criteria: A shot where separate figures or actions share a space without connecting (passing, facing away, split apart), or an isolated clue/fragment that resolves nothing; no convergence or payoff visible in frame.
signs.gloss: the situation revealed as a problem
signs.question: Why do the clues refuse to settle the situation?

diff.difference: Do parallel, heterogeneous lines of action connect only as pieces from different puzzles, so the situation they reveal remains an unanswered cipher, a sustained ellipsis?
diff.axis: where the problem is located: a priori, hidden in the situation and extracted before a considered act → [a posteriori, actions assemble heterogeneous pieces that stay a cipher] → everywhere, no originary form, the world itself a field of problems

confusions.name: Limit of the large form
confusions.flip: It is the Large-form limit instead if a single given milieu poses the question and a considered response closes it.
confusions.why_not: Ls has no originating situation; action cannot disclose one.

confusions.name: Index of equivocity
confusions.flip: It is an Index of equivocity instead if a single action points ambiguously to two possible situations and the film eventually decides between them.
confusions.why_not: Equivocity is a doubled reading of one situation; Ls is many incongruent lines whose sum is a question.

confusions.name: Forking paths
confusions.flip: It is Forking paths instead if the heterogeneous lines are memories, flashbacks within flashbacks that never reconcile.
confusions.why_not: Ls is a present-tense action structure, not a structure of recollection.

diff.counterfeit: An ensemble hyperlink film cutting between strangers looks like special homogeneity, but if the lines converge on a revealed answer (the crash, the twist) it is small-form action, not its limit.

confidence.high: Several distinct lines of action (often through women's lives in Mizoguchi) are kept heterogeneous and the film refuses the connecting answer.
confidence.medium: Multi-strand structure with only partial closure.
confidence.low: Any single shot.

diff.deamer_anchor: "all the pieces belong to different puzzles" (p. 117)

signs.name: Limit of the action-image (extreme limit)
signs.position_detail: sign of genetic forces (Deamer's own naming; Deleuze only hints at it)
signs.definition: Where the limits of the large and small forms converge and we can no longer tell which form is originary: action curves back toward the any-space-whatever and the film is permeated, from start to end, by problems - the universe as a cipher of indeterminate forces.
signs.deamer_quote: A whole world of problems, puzzles, questions and ciphers. (p. 118)
deleuze_examples: Films of Akira Kurosawa (large-form limit) and Kenji Mizoguchi (small-form limit), which Deleuze says are 're-united in the notion of the any-space-whatever' (C1: 187)
Dersu Uzala (Akira Kurosawa, 1975) - taiga as problem-space
signs.deleuze_examples_note: Deamer's Section II cites no films for this sign; examples are Deleuze's own (Cinema 1/2), supplied from knowledge of those books - verify before citing.

scenes: The Ramirez family leave the rice terraces of Benguet after being forced to sell rice at a ruinous rate.
Hand-held close-ups on Manila streets as the family are conned, lose their lodging and end in the slum; Oscar shifts rubble for a day and is cheated.
Mai works as a hostess at Charlie's while Oscar drifts into an armoured security-van job and a heist.
In the heist Oscar finds two keys: an actual one that is a ruse, and a hidden imprint, an empty void, that unlocks the future.

signs.operation: Let two incompatible modes of the same story reflect on each other until the only thing left on screen is the problem itself.
signs.shot_criteria: An indeterminate problem-space or cipher object: an empty/any-space-whatever setting, a maze, an imprint or absence standing for an answer, or a labour/social milieu shown as an open question rather than a plot situation.
signs.gloss: a whole world of problems
signs.question: Has action itself stopped being an adequate solution?

diff.difference: Is the film permeated by problems from start to end so that you can no longer tell whether they are posed by the situation or discovered by action, the world itself appearing as a field of indeterminate forces?
diff.axis: where the problem is located: a priori, hidden in the situation and extracted before a considered act → a posteriori, actions assemble heterogeneous pieces that stay a cipher → [everywhere, no originary form, the world itself a field of problems]

confusions.name: Limit of the small form
confusions.flip: It is the Small-form limit instead if the question is still traceable to the characters' actions building a cipher, with a clear action-to-situation direction.
confusions.why_not: Xl collapses the direction; the originary form is undecidable.

confusions.name: Any-space-whatever
confusions.flip: It is Any-space-whatever instead if the space is encountered as pure affect (quality/power) with no problem being worked through by action or thought.
confusions.why_not: Xl is the return to the any-space-whatever inside thought: action is still interrogating, now ungrounded.

confusions.name: Opsign
confusions.flip: It is an Opsign instead if action has actually broken down and characters only see and hear.
confusions.why_not: Xl is the limit of action-images still within the movement-image; the characters still pursue a problem.

diff.counterfeit: A sci-fi film full of enigmas (a mysterious monolith) looks like a world of problems, but if the enigma is a plot device eventually explained it is ordinary action suspense.

confidence.high: Across a whole film, situation and action both become questions and the landscape reads as a cipher (Dersu Uzala's taiga, Monsters' infected zone).
confidence.medium: Pervasive enigma with residual originary direction.
confidence.low: Single shots of a hostile, enigmatic space - indistinguishable from As.

signs.name: Rich dream
signs.position_detail: first sign of full molar composition
signs.definition: The explicitly signalled dream: entry and exit are marked, and the dream is built from overloaded technical means - dissolves, superimpositions, deframings, special effects - so the dream world is radically distinct from the real, yet its affects carry back into waking action.
signs.deamer_quote: This is a dream! - such is the formula of the rich dream (p. 123)
deleuze_examples: Entr'acte (René Clair, 1924)
Un chien andalou (Luis Buñuel and Salvador Dalí, 1929)
Sherlock Jr. (Buster Keaton, 1924) - the projectionist dreams himself into the screen
signs.deleuze_examples_note: Deamer's Section II cites no films for this sign; examples are Deleuze's own (Cinema 1/2), supplied from knowledge of those books - verify before citing.

scenes: The camera pulls back from black to reveal an eye, then a face staring into the lens, then a man in a glass tube among countless others in an impossibly vast ship.
The camera flies side to side down a corridor like a disembodied spirit.
Picard lies restrained on an operating table, his head encased in machinery; the image distorts and a drill enters his eye.
A zoom in on the sleeping Picard as he opens his eyes signals it was a dream.

signs.operation: Mark the passage into sleep with an optical transformation and fill the dream with images only trick photography can make.
signs.shot_criteria: A single shot visibly marked as dream by optical means: superimposition/double exposure, dissolve, distortion, trick-film impossibility, or a sleeper with dream imagery overlaid; plain realist shots do not count.
signs.gloss: radically distinct real world and dream world
signs.question: Can we clearly tell when the dream begins?

diff.difference: Is the passage into the dream explicitly marked and ornately made (dissolves, superimpositions, effects), with an equally marked exit, so the dream is attributed to a dreamer and recognised as dream by the viewer?
diff.axis: dream marking: [explicit, ornate entry and exit] → invisible entry, ambiguous, uncanny-but-concrete → none, the world itself dreams and includes the dreamer

confusions.name: Restrained dream
confusions.flip: It is Restrained instead if entry is a straight cut and the dream looks like concrete everyday reality with only an uncanny slip.
confusions.why_not: The rich dream announces itself: 'This is a dream!'

confusions.name: Strong destiny
confusions.flip: It is Strong destiny instead if the marked dissolve leads not into an impossible world but into a realistic past event that then determines the character's action.
confusions.why_not: A rich dream's content is impossible and abstracting; a flashback's content is a past that happened.

confusions.name: Mirrors face to face
confusions.flip: It is Mirrors face to face instead if the superimposition/reflection doesn't lead into a dreamer's world but makes actual and virtual images endlessly exchange with no one dreaming.
confusions.why_not: The rich dream has a dreamer and a return; the crystal has no subject-anchored entry or exit.

diff.counterfeit: A psychedelic music-video sequence of superimposed abstractions looks like a rich dream but lacks the dreamer-centred entry and exit, so it is formal abstraction (perhaps a gaseous perception), not a dream-image.

confidence.high: A character falls asleep, an ornate transition leads into impossible imagery, and a marked awakening returns (Sherlock Jr.).
confidence.medium: Overtly oneiric imagery with clear attribution but no marked return.
confidence.low: Heavily effected imagery without a visible dreamer.

diff.deamer_anchor: "This is a dream! – such is the formula of the rich dream" (p. 123)

signs.name: Restrained dream
signs.definition: The dream entered by a straight cut or invisible transition, resembling everyday reality but subtly impossible - an 'unhinging' between concrete objects - so that dream and real become ambiguous and the film's task becomes telling them apart.
signs.deamer_quote: Was I asleep? Am I now awake? (p. 124)
deleuze_examples: The Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie (Luis Buñuel, 1972) - dreams entered by straight cut
Late Buñuel generally: 'a perpetual unhinging' between concrete objects (C2: 58)
signs.deleuze_examples_note: Deamer's Section II cites no films for this sign; examples are Deleuze's own (Cinema 1/2), supplied from knowledge of those books - verify before citing.

scenes: As Trevor's eyes close, a book slips from his hand to the floor, a cup clatters on a coffee-bar counter, a car lighter pops on the dashboard, and he is thrown awake.
The film is shot in half-light, all murky blue-greys, around an emaciated man moving slowly with blank stares.
A co-worker named Ivan at the machine shop whom nobody else has heard of.
Post-it notes with a hangman game appear on his fridge; he spends hours scrubbing the bathroom floor.

signs.operation: Cut straight from waking to dream with no optical signal, and let one ordinary object behave slightly wrongly.
signs.shot_criteria: An unmarked, realist shot (no superimposition or dissolve) of an everyday setting or object that reads as uncanny: a drowsing or dazed figure, dim half-light, an object isolated and oddly emphasised.
signs.gloss: an ambiguity between real world and dream world
signs.question: Are we unsure whether waking has ended?

diff.difference: Is the dream entered by an invisible cut and made of concrete everyday things with one impossible unhinging, so that the film's task becomes deciding whether we are awake?
diff.axis: dream marking: explicit, ornate entry and exit → [invisible entry, ambiguous, uncanny-but-concrete] → none, the world itself dreams and includes the dreamer

confusions.name: Rich dream
confusions.flip: It is Rich instead if the entry is ornate and the imagery overtly strange.
confusions.why_not: The restrained dream hides its marking; you only learn it was a dream afterward, if ever.

confusions.name: Weak destiny
confusions.flip: It is Weak destiny instead if the unmarked intrusion turns out to be a past event (an incomplete memory) rather than an impossible present.
confusions.why_not: Restrained dream content is impossible or uncanny; weak-destiny content is a real past, just fragmentary.

confusions.name: Powers of the false
confusions.flip: It is Powers of the false instead if the ambiguity is never meant to be resolved and no dreamer anchors it: real and imaginary are undecidable in principle.
confusions.why_not: The restrained dream is still attributed to a dreamer and the film works to separate dream from real.

diff.counterfeit: A shot that looks slightly 'off' (odd colour grade, eerie silence) seems like a restrained dream, but without a later revelation or impossibility it is mood, not a dream-image.

confidence.high: A film retrospectively reveals straight-cut sequences as dreams and makes that uncertainty its subject (Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie).
confidence.medium: One unmarked dream revealed by waking, without the film thematising the doubt.
confidence.low: Any single shot: by definition nothing in the shot marks it.

diff.deamer_anchor: "Was I asleep? Am I now awake?" (p. 124)

signs.name: Movement of world
signs.definition: The implied dream with no entrance and no exit: the world itself closes around everything including the dreamer, and a movement of world (song, dance, impossible events) supplants the faltering movement of the character, so dream and real are one.
signs.deamer_quote: There is no entrance to the dream world, and no exit. (p. 125)
deleuze_examples: The Band Wagon (Vincente Minnelli, 1953)
Brigadoon (Vincente Minnelli, 1954)
Singin' in the Rain (Stanley Donen and Gene Kelly, 1952)
Top Hat (Mark Sandrich, 1935) - Astaire's dance as passage into movement of world
signs.deleuze_examples_note: Deamer's Section II cites no films for this sign; examples are Deleuze's own (Cinema 1/2), supplied from knowledge of those books - verify before citing.

scenes: Cobb's totem, a spinning top, gyrates on his kitchen table before a cut to black.
Dream cities fold: cliffs made of decaying buildings, mirrors reconstructing cityscapes, the earth curving back on itself.
Dreams nested within dreams within dreams, time stretching at each level.
The top first belonged to Mal and 'tells him nothing' - the whole film may be a dream.

signs.operation: Make the whole world move to one impossible rhythm so that no one stands outside the dream.
signs.shot_criteria: A shot where the setting itself moves with dreamlike or choreographed logic (dancing crowds, animated surroundings, rotating/folding world, perpetual spinning) and no dreamer frames it as a dream.
signs.gloss: the dream world is the real world
signs.question: What if nobody ever wakes up?

diff.difference: Is there no entry or exit at all: does the world itself carry the character along (song, dance, impossible events treated as natural) so that no one is the dreamer?
diff.axis: dream marking: explicit, ornate entry and exit → invisible entry, ambiguous, uncanny-but-concrete → [none, the world itself dreams and includes the dreamer]

confusions.name: Rich dream
confusions.flip: It is Rich instead if the number or fantasy is framed as a character's reverie with a marked return to a non-musical reality.
confusions.why_not: In movement of world the fantasy is the reality; there is nothing outside it.

confusions.name: Body of gest
confusions.flip: It is Body of gest instead if the bodies' theatricalised ceremony or gesture creates the time and nothing requires a world-movement to supplant the character's action.
confusions.why_not: Movement of world is a movement-image: the world's movement takes over the character's faltering motor act.

confusions.name: Seed and environment
confusions.flip: It is Seed and environment instead if the enchanted world is a crystal that grows from a seed and is closed, time-crystallised (e.g. a stage world that the crystal contains) rather than a dream-circuit of anamorphoses.
confusions.why_not: Movement of world is still a mental-image of the dream, with a sensory-motor subject carried along.

diff.counterfeit: A realist street scene with a busker singing looks like a musical number, but the world doesn't move the characters: song is diegetic performance, not movement of world.

confidence.high: A passerby's walk turns into dance, and the set, light and crowd move with it without any sleep frame (Singin' in the Rain title number, Band Wagon).
confidence.medium: Pervasive fantasy with vestiges of a framing reality.
confidence.low: A single dance shot without knowing whether it is framed.

diff.deamer_anchor: "There is no entrance to the dream world, and no exit." (p. 125)

signs.name: Strong destiny
signs.position_detail: first sign of full molar composition (Deamer's division of Deleuze's 'destiny')
signs.definition: The marked flashback as closed circuit of psychological causality: a character pauses, a slow dissolve or shimmer leads to a signalled past, and that past returns through affect into action, determining the character's inescapable future.
signs.deamer_quote: Strong destiny explicates the inescapable past (p. 129)
deleuze_examples: Le jour se lève (Marcel Carné, 1939) - flashbacks from the besieged room as fatal destiny
Double Indemnity (Billy Wilder, 1944) - confession frame determining the past
signs.deleuze_examples_note: Deamer's Section II cites no films for this sign; examples are Deleuze's own (Cinema 1/2), supplied from knowledge of those books - verify before citing.

section3.film: The Secret in Their Eyes (Juan José Campanella, 2009)
scenes: Espósito, face in darkness, slowly pushes open an old wooden door and enters a hidden space.
One doorway has makeshift, bent iron bars leading to a room with a bricked-up window; another opens on a brightly lit room where Morales stands with his back turned.
Through a small opening in the improvised cell shuffles a broken, balding old man - the killer, held for 25 years.
The retired agent sets out to novelise 1974, structuring the film as present-past-present.

signs.operation: Hold on a face in the present, dissolve slowly into a marked past, and return with that past driving the next act.
signs.shot_criteria: One pole of a flashback circuit: a present-tense figure pausing in reverie (ideally as a dissolve begins), or a visibly 'marked' past image (soft focus, glow, monochrome, slow motion); or an object/space from the past confronted in the present.
signs.gloss: a flashback to the past determines the future
signs.question: Does the remembered past command what happens next?

diff.difference: Does a marked flashback (pause, dissolve, monochrome, reverb) return to the present and pass through affect into an action it determines, closing a causal circuit?
diff.axis: how far the flashback travels into the present: [through affect into action (closed causal circuit)] → into affect only, a clue to be reconstructed → replaces perception, the past explored for itself

confusions.name: Weak destiny
confusions.flip: It is Weak destiny instead if the flashback is unmarked or incomplete and settles into the present's mood without yet driving an act.
confusions.why_not: Strong destiny's past is clear and it fuels a decisive act.

confusions.name: Rich dream
confusions.flip: It is a Rich dream instead if the marked transition opens onto impossible, transformed imagery rather than a realistic past.
confusions.why_not: Strong destiny's content is what happened.

confusions.name: Sheets of the past
confusions.flip: It is Sheets of the past instead if we move among coexisting regions of the past, none decisive, with no single recollection closing a circuit to action.
confusions.why_not: Strong destiny uses the past to explain; sheets explore the past as virtual coexistence.

diff.counterfeit: A dissolve to a nostalgic childhood scene looks like strong destiny but is merely a memory-illustration if it doesn't determine any action in the present.

confidence.high: Marked flashback structure whose past explains a present fatal act (Le jour se lève, Double Indemnity).
confidence.medium: Marked flashback with affective payoff but loose causal link.
confidence.low: The single transition shot alone.

diff.deamer_anchor: "allows the recollection to pass through the affect and into action" (p. 131)

signs.name: Weak destiny
signs.position_detail: secondary sign of composition (Deamer's division of Deleuze's 'destiny')
signs.definition: Flashbacks that no longer determine the future but saturate present affects: ambiguous, incomplete, unmarked, perhaps belonging to several characters, the past is a clue to an ellipsis in the present that must be reconstructed before any future is possible.
signs.deamer_quote: It is as if the past is a clue to an ellipsis in the present (p. 129)
signs.deleuze_examples_note: None: Deleuze names only a general sign 'destiny'; the strong/weak split is Deamer's own, and Section II gives no films.

scenes: In the film's present Maria is stranded on a dirt track, then rides home in a rusty old bus while flashbacks unfold.
At night Maria shows new field workers bare concrete cells lit by a single torch, points out a water pump, and retires to her whitewashed villa.
The French army withdraws; gangs of youths take up arms and a child army invades the coffee plantation.
Maria finds a ram's bloody head as a warning, tries to hide it, and fails to wipe the blood from her hands.

signs.operation: Slip into the past without a transition, let the flashback wander to other characters, and leave the present waiting in transit.
signs.shot_criteria: A present-tense figure in suspended transit or waiting (road, bus, stranded), or an unanchored, unsignalled fragment of past violence/history that could belong to anyone; no clear optical flashback marker.
signs.gloss: the content of the flashback permeates affects
signs.question: Does memory color the present without dictating it?

diff.difference: Is the flashback ambiguous, incomplete or shared, so it saturates present feeling as a clue to an ellipsis that must be reconstructed before any action can follow?
diff.axis: how far the flashback travels into the present: through affect into action (closed causal circuit) → [into affect only, a clue to be reconstructed] → replaces perception, the past explored for itself

confusions.name: Strong destiny
confusions.flip: It is Strong destiny instead if the flashback is clearly marked and complete and directly produces an action.
confusions.why_not: Weak destiny stalls action; the past is a puzzle, not a cause.

confusions.name: Restrained dream
confusions.flip: It is a Restrained dream instead if the unmarked intrusion is impossible rather than a past event.
confusions.why_not: Weak destiny content is real past, fragmentary.

confusions.name: Sheets of the past
confusions.flip: It is Sheets of the past instead if no ellipsis is ultimately resolved and the film moves among coexisting ages of the past without a present to rescue.
confusions.why_not: Weak destiny still aims at reconstruction and resolution.

diff.counterfeit: A non-linear edit that shuffles chronology for suspense looks like weak destiny, but if it isn't a character's memory saturating affect, it is simply narration order.

confidence.high: Fragmentary flashbacks from one or several characters are revisited and pieced together (White Material).
confidence.medium: Unmarked memory fragments that are eventually explained.
confidence.low: Single shot; cannot even establish that it is a memory.

diff.deamer_anchor: "consents the recollection to pass into the affect" (p. 131)

signs.name: Forking paths
signs.definition: Memory as fragmentation of linearity: flashbacks within flashbacks and circuits that fork within themselves 'like a split hair', exploring the past for itself as an inexplicable secret, so that psychological causality is exposed as a ruse.
signs.deamer_quote: Flashbacks within flashbacks within flashbacks ... or irresolvable flashbacks (p. 130)
deleuze_examples: All About Eve (Joseph L. Mankiewicz, 1950)
A Letter to Three Wives (Joseph L. Mankiewicz, 1949)
The Barefoot Contessa (Joseph L. Mankiewicz, 1954) - forking multi-narrator flashbacks
signs.deleuze_examples_note: Deamer's Section II cites no films for this sign; examples are Deleuze's own (Cinema 1/2), supplied from knowledge of those books - verify before citing.

scenes: In the ballroom of a ghost ocean liner, Jess aims a shotgun at another Jess as the camera circles the doppelgangers.
After a storm capsizes the yacht, survivors cling to the upturned hull until a liner emerges from the sea mist.
Jess studies her bruised body in a mirror and the camera passes through the glass to join her reflection.
Jess wakes washed up on a Miami beach on the morning before the trip, and the loop begins again.

signs.operation: Build loops that fork within themselves: double the figure, pass through the mirror, and return to the start changed.
signs.shot_criteria: A shot of doubling or looping: a figure and its double/reflection in the same frame, infinite mirror regress, multiple exposure of one person, a literal forking path, or the looping sea/ship imagery of the Section III scenes.
signs.gloss: a matrix of irresolvable flashbacks
signs.question: Which past, if any, actually explains the present?

diff.difference: Do flashbacks fork within flashbacks, irreconcilably, so the past is explored for its own sake as an inexplicable secret and psychological causality is shown to be a ruse?
diff.axis: how far the flashback travels into the present: through affect into action (closed causal circuit) → into affect only, a clue to be reconstructed → [replaces perception, the past explored for itself]

confusions.name: Weak destiny
confusions.flip: It is Weak destiny instead if the fragments eventually cohere and resolve the present ellipsis.
confusions.why_not: Forking paths never reconcile; the secret remains.

confusions.name: Sheets of the past
confusions.flip: It is Sheets of the past instead if the forking no longer passes through flashbacks at all but directly through coexistent regions of pure past, with no present anchoring the recollections.
confusions.why_not: Forking paths is still a movement-image of memory: actualised flashbacks returning to a present.

confusions.name: Powers of the false
confusions.flip: It is Powers of the false instead if the contradictory versions are not memories of a secret but forgeries that make truth itself undecidable.
confusions.why_not: Forking paths assumes a past that happened, just unreachable.

diff.counterfeit: A multi-narrator courtroom film looks like forking paths, but if the versions are adjudicated and one truth emerges, it is weak destiny.

confidence.high: Nested multi-narrator flashbacks whose accounts do not reconcile (Mankiewicz).
confidence.medium: Nested flashbacks with only partial contradiction.
confidence.low: Any single shot.

diff.deamer_anchor: "the movie explores the past for itself" (p. 130)

signs.name: Mark
signs.position_detail: first sign of full molar composition
signs.definition: A habitual series of images, each interpretable by the others; perceived objects that repeat at least three times until the series forces itself into consciousness and becomes the chain of thought that constitutes the narration.
signs.deamer_quote: there must be at least three such images to form a series (p. 133)
deleuze_examples: Hitchcock's relation-image generally (C1: 200-203)
Strangers on a Train (Alfred Hitchcock, 1951) - the exchanged crime as chain of relations
signs.deleuze_examples_note: Deamer's Section II cites no films for this sign; examples are Deleuze's own (Cinema 1/2), supplied from knowledge of those books - verify before citing.

scenes: An obese man found bound and force-fed to death; 'gluttony' later found scraped in grease behind the fridge.
A lawyer's office with 'greed' written in blood on the floor and an upside-down picture hiding fingerprints.
A man tied to a bed for a year - the third murder that confirms the series (Sloth).
The Seven Deadly Sins listed in chalk on an old school blackboard, crossed off one by one.

signs.operation: Repeat one kind of image three times so the audience starts reading every new shot as the next term.
signs.shot_criteria: One visible term of a series: a numbered/listed item, one of several near-identical scenes or objects, or a repeated inscription; strongest if the frame itself shows repetition (rows, lists, sets of three).
signs.gloss: the relation between a habitual series of images
signs.question: What recurring thing has become meaningful because it repeats?

diff.difference: Can you point to at least three occurrences of the same image or motif that the characters or viewer come to read as one habitual series with a meaning to be deciphered?
diff.axis: relation-image: habit → aberration → abstraction; mark (habitual series, full composition) / demark (aberration from the series, secondary composition) / symbol (concrete object bearing abstract relations, genesis)

confusions.name: Demark
confusions.flip: It is a demark instead if the shot shows one instance that breaks the established series: wrong place, wrong form, wrong time.
confusions.why_not: A mark shot confirms the series; it adds one more regular term and nothing in it is out of pattern.

confusions.name: Mise en abyme
confusions.flip: It is mise en abyme instead if the repetition nests one image inside another (a picture of the film within the film) instead of lining up terms in time.
confusions.why_not: The mark's repetitions follow one another as separate perceived objects in the present, not images framed inside images.

confusions.name: Sheets of the past
confusions.flip: It is sheets of the past instead if the recurring image returns the viewer to different, non-chronological layers of the past rather than building a logical inference.
confusions.why_not: The mark stays in the present and in logic ('because', 'therefore'); its recurrences point forward to an interpretation, not back into strata of time.

diff.counterfeit: A montage of three similar establishing shots of a city is repetition without inference: nobody treats the series as a clue, so it is style, not a mark.

confidence.high: Three or more recurrences across a sequence are explicitly noticed or pursued by a character (a detective lining up crime scenes).
confidence.medium: The recurrences are clear to the viewer but the film never marks them as something to read.
confidence.low: A single shot containing one instance of a motif; the series exists only across the film.

diff.deamer_anchor: 'at least three such images to form a series' (p.133)

signs.name: Demark
signs.definition: An aberration in an established habitual series: one term leaps outside the web or contradicts it, producing a shock that reorients the chain of thought and becomes the new question of the narration.
signs.deamer_quote: any aberration in the series becomes significant. A shock (p. 134)
deleuze_examples: Foreign Correspondent (Alfred Hitchcock, 1940) - the windmill turning against the wind
North by Northwest (Alfred Hitchcock, 1959) - the crop-duster where there are no crops
signs.deleuze_examples_note: Deamer's Section II cites no films for this sign; examples are Deleuze's own (Cinema 1/2), supplied from knowledge of those books - verify before citing.

section3.film: Doctor Who - The Day of the Doctor (Nick Hurran, 2013)
scenes: Gallifrey besieged by the Dalek army; the general exclaims at three Doctors appearing at once.
The unnamed War Doctor, the incarnation who refused the name, prepares the doomsday weapon The Moment.
The Tenth and Eleventh Doctors are brought to confront their hidden predecessor.
Buried (Deamer's other example): among three sets of things in the coffin, a snake enters and leaves - the demark.

signs.operation: Set up a regular series, then let one term appear where it cannot belong.
signs.shot_criteria: A regular series visible in frame with one element out of place (out of step, wrong color, wrong direction, missing, or an object/animal where it cannot belong); the shot must show both the norm and the aberration.
signs.gloss: an aberration in the series of habitual images
signs.question: What breaks the pattern?

diff.difference: Does the shot show a known term of an established series appearing out of place or contradicting that series, so that the aberration itself shocks thought?
diff.axis: relation-image: habit → aberration → abstraction; mark (habitual series, full composition) / demark (aberration from the series, secondary composition) / symbol (concrete object bearing abstract relations, genesis)

confusions.name: Mark
confusions.flip: It is a mark instead if the term appears where and as the series predicts.
confusions.why_not: The demark is defined by violation; a conforming instance only restates the series.

confusions.name: Index of equivocity
confusions.flip: It is an index of equivocity instead if the shot presents one action that can be read two ways, with no prior habitual series being broken.
confusions.why_not: The demark needs a pattern set up earlier in the film; its shock comes from the pattern, not from an ambiguity in the action.

confusions.name: Powers of the false
confusions.flip: It is powers of the false instead if the break undoes the truth of the whole narration (a storyteller exposed, versions multiplying) and no pattern is left to restore.
confusions.why_not: A demark breaks a series inside a logic that still holds, and thought re-orients; the powers of the false erode the ground of truth itself.

diff.counterfeit: A sudden jump scare breaks expectations but belongs to no series the film has built; it is a shock to the body, not a demark to thought.

confidence.high: The film first establishes a series (three or more terms), then shows an aberrant term to which a character visibly reacts by rethinking.
confidence.medium: The series is established but the aberration is subtle and only the viewer registers it.
confidence.low: An isolated odd object in a frame without knowledge of the series it breaks.

diff.deamer_anchor: 'any aberration in the series becomes significant. A shock' (p.134)

signs.name: Symbol
signs.definition: An abstract relation carried by a concrete object: demarks extracted from different series coalesce in one thing, which becomes a node bearing various relations (or variations of one) and so expresses an idea, belief or concept.
signs.deamer_quote: an object expressing ideas, beliefs, concepts (Fig. II.33, p. 135)
deleuze_examples: The 39 Steps (Alfred Hitchcock, 1935) - the handcuffs
Notorious (Alfred Hitchcock, 1946) - the key
Suspicion (Alfred Hitchcock, 1941) - the glowing glass of milk
signs.deleuze_examples_note: Deamer's Section II cites no films for this sign; examples are Deleuze's own (Cinema 1/2), supplied from knowledge of those books - verify before citing.

scenes: Black screen, breathing, then a zippo flame reveals Paul Conroy buried alive in a wooden coffin.
Close-ups and extreme close-ups of sweat, blood and dirty fingernails, lit by lighter, mobile phone and torch in abstract patterns of light and dark.
A snake enters the coffin and leaves it again - a vertical element crossing a horizontal plane, the promise of a way out.
The coffin itself becomes the symbol, as if the character were placed inside Hitchcock's McGuffin (the package in the train's baggage rack).

signs.operation: Isolate one concrete object and let every relation in the film pass through it.
signs.shot_criteria: A single concrete object isolated and charged by framing or light (insert close-up, object in darkness, object as the centre of a composition), strong enough to carry meaning beyond its function.
signs.gloss: an object expressing ideas, beliefs, concepts
signs.question: What idea is being thought through this thing?

diff.difference: Is a single concrete object held on screen as the knot where several separate threads of the film's relations meet, so that it carries an idea, belief or concept rather than a use or a desire?
diff.axis: relation-image: habit → aberration → abstraction; mark (habitual series, full composition) / demark (aberration from the series, secondary composition) / symbol (concrete object bearing abstract relations, genesis)

confusions.name: Fetish
confusions.flip: It is a fetish instead if the object is invested with drive (grabbed, hoarded, torn at, possessed) in an originary world of impulse.
confusions.why_not: The symbol is thought about, not clutched: its value is abstract relation, not an object of predatory drive.

confusions.name: Mark
confusions.flip: It is a mark instead if the object only recurs as one term of a single habitual series.
confusions.why_not: The symbol gathers demarks from several different series into one object; a mark belongs to one line of repetition.

confusions.name: Lectosign
confusions.flip: It is a lectosign instead if what must be read is the whole film's image, narration and narrative with no single object given as the key.
confusions.why_not: The symbol offers a key object that settles meaning inside the movement-image; a lectosign offers no key, only a relinking the viewer must do.

diff.counterfeit: A close-up of a wedding ring that a character pawns is a prop in action (a means), not a symbol, unless the film has made it carry several distinct relations.

confidence.high: The object recurs across several distinct plot lines and is finally isolated in a way that condenses them (the lighter, the phone, the coffin).
confidence.medium: The object is visibly singled out and plausibly abstract, but only one relation is established.
confidence.low: A single insert of an object, which could equally be a fetish, a prop or a mark.

diff.deamer_anchor: 'an object expressing ideas, beliefs, concepts' (Fig. II.33, p.135)

signs.name: Opsign
signs.image_type: Opsign / pure actual optical situation (zeroness of the time-image, optical side)
signs.definition: The actual visual image cut off from its motor extension: what is seen no longer passes into feeling or action, but stays on screen as a pure, de-differenciated optical situation that the look can only register. Together with its sound twin, the sonsign, it is the zero point from which every other time-image grows.
signs.deamer_quote: ‘Everything returns to the purest zeroness – everything can begin again’ (p.138)
deleuze_examples: Europa '51 (Roberto Rossellini, 1952) - the bourgeois woman stares at factory workers: 'I thought I was seeing convicts'
Umberto D. (Vittorio De Sica, 1952) - the young maid alone in the morning kitchen, grinding coffee, looking at her belly
Stromboli (Roberto Rossellini, 1950) - the woman facing the volcano and the tuna catch
Late Spring (Yasujiro Ozu, 1949) - the still shot of a vase in a darkened room
L'Eclisse (Michelangelo Antonioni, 1962) - closing sequence of empty street corners
signs.deleuze_examples_source: Deamer's Section II (pp.138-172) cites no films for these signs; examples are Deleuze's own from Cinema 2, supplied from Cinema 2 rather than from Deamer.

scenes: A barnacled chunk of driftwood rolls in the surf at the tideline, breaks in two, and one piece drifts out of frame while the camera stays put.
A fixed camera on a stone seaside promenade with double railings; joggers, dog walkers and strollers cross, leaving the frame empty at times, until four old men with canes stop to chat.
Dogs sleep as dark blobs on a distant beach while the morning light bleaches sky, sea and sand into one white field.
The full moon reflected on black water at night wobbles and fades as rain and toads fill the soundtrack.

signs.operation: Fix the camera on a place, object or onlooker where nothing is meant to happen and hold the image until what is seen stops leading anywhere.
signs.shot_criteria: Judged on the image alone: a static or near-static shot of a place, object, light-change or crowd with no protagonist pursuing a goal, or an onlooker frozen in pure seeing; whatever moves (water, light, passers-by, animals) just happens and resolves nothing, and the next cut is not motivated by it. Sound is irrelevant to the test; the shot must hold with the sound off.
signs.gloss: the zeroness of the time-image: a pure optical situation
signs.question: Can this sight still be discharged into action?

diff.difference: With the sound off, is the image something to be seen and nothing more: no one's goal organises it, what moves in it resolves nothing, and the look is not converted into action?
diff.axis: modality: optical ↔ sound

confusions.name: Sonsign
confusions.flip: It is (also or only) a sonsign if the sound carries the situation, holding the scene while the image is neutral, dark or incidental.
confusions.why_not: A typical opsign still stands with the sound off; its pure situation is visual.

confusions.name: Any-space-whatever
confusions.flip: It is an any-space-whatever instead if the disconnected space works as the ground of affect (shadow, colour, emptiness charging a feeling in a movement-image film) and the film then goes back into action.
confusions.why_not: The opsign is the any-space-whatever after the movement-image has collapsed: the space no longer charges a later affect or act but is simply seen.

confusions.name: Quotidian
confusions.flip: It is the quotidian instead if everyday banality is framed as a critical figure (a reflection on routine) inside a film still driven by situation → action.
confusions.why_not: The opsign does not comment on the everyday; the look just stalls on it, and the film does not return to a plot the banality serves.

diff.counterfeit: A long static establishing shot of an empty street before a chase is a pause, not an opsign, because the next shot cashes it into action.

confidence.high: A long take with nobody pursuing anything and a whole film that refuses to recover sensory-motor links (Five, late Antonioni).
confidence.medium: A single dead-time shot or onlooker frozen in seeing inside a film whose plot partly resumes.
confidence.low: A still landscape seen in isolation: without the next cut you cannot tell a pure optical situation from an establishing shot.

diff.deamer_anchor: 'pure actual optical and sound situations' (p.138); Deamer treats op/son jointly

signs.name: Sonsign
signs.image_type: Sonsign / pure actual sound situation (zeroness of the time-image, sound side)
signs.definition: The actual sound image cut off from its motor extension: a sound that is itself the situation rather than score, dialogue or cue for action. It is heard and holds the scene, while neither the listener nor the image converts it into a response. It is the aural twin of the opsign and can occur without one, over a neutral image, a frozen listener or black.
signs.deamer_quote: ‘actual on-screen de-differenciated visual and audio images’ (p.138)
deleuze_examples: Mr. Hulot's Holiday / Playtime (Jacques Tati, 1953 / 1967): noises such as the flapping dining-room door and the buzzing, clicking modern building stand as situations in their own right (recalled from Cinema 2, ch.1; not in Deamer)
India Song (Marguerite Duras, 1975): voices off, never synchronised with the bodies on screen, form a sound situation of their own (recalled from Cinema 2, ch.9; not in Deamer)
Fortini/Cani (Jean-Marie Straub and Daniele Huillet, 1976): a text read aloud over empty landscapes, the speech act kept apart from the visual layer (recalled from Cinema 2, ch.9; not in Deamer)

Umberto D. (Vittorio De Sica, 1952): the maid's morning kitchen, where tap, coffee grinder and door noises carry no action (recalled from Cinema 2, ch.1; Deleuze stresses the optical side there; not in Deamer)
signs.deleuze_examples_source: Deamer's Section II (pp.138-144) cites no films and treats opsigns and sonsigns jointly; these examples are recalled from Deleuze's Cinema 2 and should be checked against it. The split of sonsign into its own element is this project's, not Deamer's.

scenes: On the promenade, four old men with canes stop to talk, but their speech is never heard. The roar of the breaking waves takes its place, so the talk turns into a sound situation with no content (p.302).

The white noise of the sea runs through the first four sequences as a constant bed, including the one where the dogs lie on the beach and the light bleaches out. It is an environment you hear and never a cue (p.304).

'Moon on Water, Serenade of Toads' opens in near silence on a black screen. A slow crescendo of toads and a storm builds 'in time' into the roar of nature, and it grows on its own while the image has nearly vanished (p.304).
Plops of raindrops and lightning hit the black water and blur the moon's reflection, so the sound of the storm stands in for any event (p.304).

signs.operation: Take away the action and let a sound hold the scene: starve the image, or freeze the listener, until what is heard is the situation instead of an accompaniment or a signal to act.
signs.shot_criteria: From the image alone (visual search), look for either (a) a listener frozen before an unseen or distant source, head tilted or turned, not moving to answer, or (b) a sound source isolated with no action attached: bells, loudspeakers, radio, phonograph, sirens, whistles, machinery running unattended, rain on water, surf, frogs or birds calling, crowds heard off an empty frame. It can also be a near-empty or dark image where sound would have to carry everything. After that, a listen must confirm three things: the sound stands alone (not music scoring, not dialogue driving plot), it goes on longer than any action it could trigger, and nobody responds to it.
signs.gloss: the zeroness of the time-image: a pure sound situation
signs.question: Does this sound stand alone as a situation, answered by no action?

diff.difference: With the image covered, does a sound hold the scene as a situation in itself, not score, not plot-driving dialogue, not a cue someone answers?
diff.axis: modality: optical ↔ sound

confusions.name: Opsign
confusions.flip: It is an opsign instead if the shot still stands with the sound off and the sound is just ambient support.
confusions.why_not: In a sonsign the image is neutral, dark or frozen; take the sound away and the situation disappears.

confusions.name: Mark
confusions.flip: It is a mark instead if the sound recurs (a bell, a whistle, a ringtone) as a habitual series that characters interpret as a clue.
confusions.why_not: The sonsign does not point anywhere; it is heard, not deciphered, and nothing is inferred from it.

confusions.name: Binomial
confusions.flip: It is an action-image sign (binomial: situation → response) instead if the sound triggers a response: the alarm makes someone run, the phone is answered, the whistle ends the shift.
confusions.why_not: A sonsign has no motor extension; the listener stays frozen or absent and the sound outlasts any reaction.

diff.counterfeit: A loud siren over a fire-engine chase is diegetic sound but not a sonsign: it drives the action and the image carries the situation.

confidence.high: Sound plays over black or near-black, or over a static image, and grows on its own terms for a long duration (Five's toads and storm).
confidence.medium: A frozen listener before an off-screen or distant sound source, confirmed by listening.
confidence.low: Any judgement made from the image without its soundtrack; at most a sonsign candidate.

diff.deamer_anchor: 'actual on-screen de-differenciated visual and audio images' (p.138)

signs.name: Mirrors face to face
signs.definition: The first crystal-image: one actual image splits into many perspectives through mirrors, reflections and doubles, so the body and its setting show up in fragments, duplicates and distortions, and you can no longer tell the actual from the virtual.
signs.deamer_quote: ‘depicted space is complex, the body is a crystal’ (p.147)
deleuze_examples: The Lady from Shanghai (Orson Welles, 1947) - the hall-of-mirrors shoot-out
Citizen Kane (Orson Welles, 1941) - Kane walks between two facing mirrors, multiplied to infinity
Lola Montes (Max Ophuls, 1955) - the circus ring and its reflecting spectacle
The Golden Coach (Jean Renoir, 1952) - mirrors of stage and court
signs.deleuze_examples_source: Deamer's Section II (pp.138-172) cites no films for these signs; examples are Deleuze's own from Cinema 2, supplied from Cinema 2 rather than from Deamer.

scenes: On the subway Nina sees her own reflection in the blackened window, then through the glass doors between cars a double of herself in a black coat.
Nina warms up at a threefold standing mirror in the apartment's front room.
A communal dressing room of plate mirrors and small round table mirrors multiplies the ballet dancers.
The costumer's room makes almost endless copies of Nina; on opening night her dressing-room mirror is shattered and bloody.

signs.operation: Put two reflecting surfaces into the shot so that the body appears more than once and one copy is not quite the original.
signs.shot_criteria: A body or place visibly doubled, multiplied or distorted by a mirror, window, water or other reflecting surface inside a single frame; a plain unreflected figure does not count.
signs.gloss: fragments, duplicates and distortions
signs.question: Which image is original?

diff.difference: Does one body or thing appear in the same shot as several reflections or doubles at once (facing, angled or distorting mirrors, glass), so that actual and virtual can no longer be told apart?
diff.axis: hyalosign: which moment of the present the actual image exchanges with its virtual; mirrors (the present multiplied: simultaneous doubles) / limpid-opaque (the passing present: one side clears as the other clouds) / seed-environment (the future: a small image enclosing the world it will become, genesis)

confusions.name: Limpid and opaque
confusions.flip: It is limpid and opaque instead if, over time, one side clears as the other clouds (a reflection fades as the room behind the glass appears, or the reverse).
confusions.why_not: Mirrors face to face multiply simultaneously; there is no passage from clear to obscure, just many images at once.

confusions.name: Mise en abyme
confusions.flip: It is mise en abyme instead if the image framed within the image is a representation (a painting, a play, a screen) reflecting the story critically.
confusions.why_not: In the mirror image the doubles are the body itself dispersed, not a representation of the plot within the plot.

confusions.name: Theatrical figure
confusions.flip: It is a theatrical figure instead if the mirror is just a stage prop for a role or disguise being performed and then taken off.
confusions.why_not: Mirrors face to face make the self crystalline and fragmented; there is no 'real' self to return to after the play.

diff.counterfeit: A character checking their make-up in one bathroom mirror is a single reflection serving continuity, not a crystal: nothing is multiplied or made indiscernible.

confidence.high: Multiple simultaneous reflections of one body where the real body is hard or impossible to locate (hall of mirrors, facing mirrors).
confidence.medium: One or two reflections that visibly split or distort the figure.
confidence.low: A single mirror shot used for ordinary framing.

diff.deamer_anchor: 'depicted space is complex, the body is a crystal' (p.147)

signs.name: Limpid and opaque
signs.definition: The second crystal-image: two sides of one image keep swapping places, so that as one becomes clear and visible the other goes dark, the way an actor turns into a role and back. The present is always passing into an opaque past.
signs.deamer_quote: ‘An image is limpid – luminous, clear – for a moment’ (p.147)
deleuze_examples: The Golden Coach (Jean Renoir, 1952) - Camilla between stage and life: 'where does the theatre end, where does life begin?'
The Rules of the Game (Jean Renoir, 1939) - the chateau's masquerade and the actor's transparent and opaque faces
Lola Montes (Max Ophuls, 1955) - the circus reenactment of her life
8 1/2 (Federico Fellini, 1963) - film-within-film spectacle
signs.deleuze_examples_source: Deamer's Section II (pp.138-172) cites no films for these signs; examples are Deleuze's own from Cinema 2, supplied from Cinema 2 rather than from Deamer.

scenes: Six participants sit on plastic chairs in a bare warehouse while the method-acting coach leads them into their inner lives.
Lian plays King Lear alone to an empty theatre.
James is knifed outside his house by a gang of teenagers in his self-made short.
Ash's short turns violently brutal, so the 'real' Ash and the played Ash replace each other.

signs.operation: Cut between a person rehearsing and the same person in the finished role until you can't tell which is performing.
signs.shot_criteria: A frame that holds two states of one image at once: a person between self and role (rehearsal, costume, bare stage), or something visibly half-there (seen through translucent glass, fog, superimposition, or a screen lit from behind).
signs.gloss: the exchange of the actual and virtual
signs.question: Which side of the image is becoming real?

diff.difference: During the shot or scene, does one face of the image clear (becomes visible or real) while the other clouds (becomes obscure or virtual), so that the two sides keep changing places?
diff.axis: hyalosign: which moment of the present the actual image exchanges with its virtual; mirrors (the present multiplied: simultaneous doubles) / limpid-opaque (the passing present: one side clears as the other clouds) / seed-environment (the future: a small image enclosing the world it will become, genesis)

confusions.name: Mirrors face to face
confusions.flip: It is mirrors face to face instead if the doubles are all present at once and nothing passes from clear to opaque.
confusions.why_not: The limpid/opaque is a passage in time (an exchange), not a simultaneous multiplication.

confusions.name: Powers of the false
confusions.flip: It is powers of the false instead if what alternates is the truth of the whole story (a performer versus a real witness, with no fact left) rather than two faces of one image.
confusions.why_not: The limpid/opaque exchanges actual and virtual within an image or scene; the powers of the false dissolve truth across the narration.

confusions.name: Rich dream
confusions.flip: It is a rich dream instead if the obscure side is marked as a character's dream with a clear waking frame around it.
confusions.why_not: In the limpid/opaque the virtual is not assigned to a dreamer's head; reality and virtual pass into each other without a frame.

diff.counterfeit: A cross-dissolve from one scene to the next moves from one actual to another actual and does not exchange an image with its own virtual.

confidence.high: A performer or scene that visibly passes between 'real' and 'performed' in duration, both sides kept in play (actor/role, glass that is window then mirror).
confidence.medium: A lighting or focus change that turns a reflection into transparency, where the narrative supports the doubling.
confidence.low: A still frame, which cannot show the passage.

diff.deamer_anchor: 'limpid … for a moment, but in passing becomes opaque' (p.147)

signs.name: Seed and environment
signs.definition: The genetic crystal-image, oriented toward the future: a small actual object or moment contains a whole setting that has not appeared yet, or a large dispersed setting points back to a seed that can't be pinned down.
signs.deamer_quote: ‘as if it were a miniature scene within a globe of opaque glass’ (p.149)
deleuze_examples: Citizen Kane (Orson Welles, 1941) - the snow-filled glass globe that drops from Kane's hand
Solaris (Andrei Tarkovsky, 1972) - the ocean as crystallising environment
And the Ship Sails On (Federico Fellini, 1983) - the ship as crystal in formation
The Leopard (Luchino Visconti, 1963) - the aristocratic world as crystal in decomposition
signs.deleuze_examples_source: Deamer's Section II (pp.138-172) cites no films for these signs; examples are Deleuze's own from Cinema 2, supplied from Cinema 2 rather than from Deamer.

scenes: At breakfast a children's TV cartoon shows farm animals learning about viruses: the seed of Caden's illness and of the play.
Caden rents a colossal disused warehouse and fills it with sprawling sets that grow into a replica of the city outside.
Adele paints tiny images that can only be seen through a magnifying glass, and they get smaller as she vanishes.
Old Caden with a cane walks through graffitied, ruined set-streets past a clock spray-painted on brick that reads 7:45.

signs.operation: Show a small object that holds a whole world in miniature, then let the full-size world grow out of it.
signs.shot_criteria: A shot where a small bounded thing (globe, model, seed, crystal, miniature, tiny painting, screen) visibly contains or foreshadows a larger environment, or a vast built environment that looks like it grew from one.
signs.gloss: (virtual/actual) seed ↔ (actual/virtual) environment
signs.question: What future world lies virtually inside this image?

diff.difference: Is there a small enclosed image (a snow globe, model, miniature stage, a drop, a crystal) that contains in germ the world that surrounds it or will grow from it, with seed and environment reversible?
diff.axis: hyalosign: which moment of the present the actual image exchanges with its virtual; mirrors (the present multiplied: simultaneous doubles) / limpid-opaque (the passing present: one side clears as the other clouds) / seed-environment (the future: a small image enclosing the world it will become, genesis)

confusions.name: Limpid and opaque
confusions.flip: It is limpid and opaque instead if two faces trade places over time without one containing the other.
confusions.why_not: Seed and environment is a relation of enclosure and growth (small holds large), not alternation.

confusions.name: Mise en abyme
confusions.flip: It is mise en abyme instead if the inner image is a critical reflection (story within story) that the plot comments on and then leaves.
confusions.why_not: The seed is not a commentary but a germ: the environment grows out of it or collapses back into it, and you cannot say which is primary.

confusions.name: Cinema of the brain
confusions.flip: It is cinema of the brain instead if the whole set or world is laid out as a mental map with no enclosed miniature seed.
confusions.why_not: The seed/environment keeps a germinal object inside the world; the brain-cinema turns the whole screen into the cerebral space.

diff.counterfeit: A model railway on a shelf in the background is décor unless the film makes the world outside behave as its expansion.

confidence.high: A miniature or enclosed image that the film explicitly grows into, or reveals itself inside (the warehouse set of a city inside the city).
confidence.medium: A prominent crystal, globe or model held in frame that echoes the surrounding space.
confidence.low: Any small object in a still, whose germinal role only the film can confirm.

diff.deamer_anchor: 'a miniature scene within a globe of opaque glass' (p.149)

signs.name: Peaks of the present
signs.definition: The first chronosign: narration is laid out as several presents happening at once, each possible alone but not together (incompossible), so the story is no longer a line of successive actions.
signs.deamer_quote: ‘the narration appears in the simultaneity of differing presents’ (p.153)
deleuze_examples: Last Year at Marienbad (Alain Resnais / Alain Robbe-Grillet, 1961) - incompatible presents of the man and the woman in the chateau garden
L'Immortelle (Alain Robbe-Grillet, 1963)
The Man Who Lies (Alain Robbe-Grillet, 1968) - the same event told in incompatible versions
signs.deleuze_examples_source: Deamer's Section II (pp.138-172) cites no films for these signs; examples are Deleuze's own from Cinema 2, supplied from Cinema 2 rather than from Deamer.

section3.film: Uncle Boonmee Who Can Recall His Past Lives (Apichatpong Weerasethakul, 2010)
scenes: After the funeral, the family both stays in the hotel room watching TV and goes out to a bar to eat, at the same moment.
The ghost of Boonmee's wife appears, translucent, at the dinner table on the farm.
His lost son comes out of the forest at night as a furry monkey ghost with glowing red eyes.
Boonmee's dream of the future is told over still photographs of Thai soldiers with civilian-clothed prisoners.

signs.operation: Show the same moment twice, happening in two ways that can't both be true, and don't choose between them.
signs.shot_criteria: A single frame that holds two presents at once: the same person twice, split screen, superimposed people, clocks showing different times, or an ordinary scene with an impossible presence sitting inside it.
signs.gloss: the heterogeneous present
signs.question: What if several presents are simultaneously valid?

diff.difference: Does the narration give several different presents at once (a present of the past, a present of the present, a present of the future) in the same event, without flashback framing to rank them?
diff.axis: chronosign: which order of time organises narration; peaks of the present (coexisting presents) / sheets of the past (coexisting strata of past, non-chronological) / powers of the false (series of time: becoming that falsifies, genesis)

confusions.name: Sheets of the past
confusions.flip: It is sheets of the past instead if the coexistence is of strata of the past explored as a memory-world, not of presents.
confusions.why_not: Peaks of the present are simultaneous nows (the same moment lived as several), not layers dug back into.

confusions.name: Forking paths
confusions.flip: It is forking paths instead if the alternatives are subordinated to one present (a flashback that explains, or possibilities that resolve into one timeline).
confusions.why_not: In peaks of the present no version is the frame; the presents are incompossible yet all actual.

confusions.name: Limit of large form
confusions.flip: It is the limit of large form instead if parallel lines of action converge in a race to a decisive duel.
confusions.why_not: The peaks do not converge on an act; they stay heterogeneous and unresolved.

diff.counterfeit: Cross-cutting between two characters in different places at the same clock time is simultaneity of space, not of heterogeneous presents.

confidence.high: The same moment is replayed with incompatible versions, or past/future beings share the present scene without explanation (ghosts at the dinner table).
confidence.medium: Temporal indicators clash within a scene but the film half-explains them.
confidence.low: A single shot; the sign lives in narration across shots.

diff.deamer_anchor: 'narration appears in the simultaneity of differing presents' (p.153)

signs.name: Sheets of the past
signs.definition: The second chronosign: the film moves around inside a pure past made of coexisting layers, jumping between them out of chronological order, with echoes and resonance taking the place of cause and effect.
signs.deamer_quote: ‘There is no cause and effect, just events that ricochet, backwards and forwards’ (p.154)
deleuze_examples: Citizen Kane (Orson Welles, 1941) - witnesses' flashbacks, each a sheet of Kane's past; depth-of-field as memory
Hiroshima mon amour (Alain Resnais, 1959) - Nevers and Hiroshima as two coexisting pasts
Je t'aime, je t'aime (Alain Resnais, 1968) - the man jumping between moments of one year
Mr. Arkadin (Orson Welles, 1955) - an investigation through sheets of a man's past
signs.deleuze_examples_source: Deamer's Section II (pp.138-172) cites no films for these signs; examples are Deleuze's own from Cinema 2, supplied from Cinema 2 rather than from Deamer.

scenes: The narrator and the Marquis watch Peter the Great's chambers through dark glass and old stone, the Tsar's anger muffled and out of reach.
After a dark spiral staircase, a lateral track passes men turning wooden stage-wheels, soldiers in armour, dancers and an orchestra pit into Catherine the Great's theatre.
The travellers jump between sheets: Leningrad under siege, the Persian ambassador at court, Nicholas II's family at breakfast.
At the end the Neva has flooded and the Hermitage floats like an ark on the waters of time.

signs.operation: Track one long unbroken shot through a building where each room belongs to a different decade.
signs.shot_criteria: A shot through a space layered with accumulated time (palace galleries, museum halls, archives, storerooms, ruins, old photographs) where different pasts sit side by side, ideally deep focus or long tracking.
signs.gloss: the non-chronological nature of the past
signs.question: Which layer of the past are we inhabiting?

diff.difference: Does the film move between regions of the past that coexist and ricochet non-chronologically (layered periods in one space, without a present-day narrator motivating each return)?
diff.axis: chronosign: which order of time organises narration; peaks of the present (coexisting presents) / sheets of the past (coexisting strata of past, non-chronological) / powers of the false (series of time: becoming that falsifies, genesis)

confusions.name: Peaks of the present
confusions.flip: It is peaks of the present instead if what coexists are nows, not strata of the past.
confusions.why_not: Sheets of the past are the past as a whole, sheet on sheet, into which the film plunges.

confusions.name: Strong destiny
confusions.flip: It is a recollection-image (strong destiny) instead if a flashback is motivated by a character's present need and returns to that present.
confusions.why_not: The sheets are not summoned to explain the present; there is no cause and effect, only ricochet.

confusions.name: Milieu
confusions.flip: It is a milieu instead if the historical setting is a determining environment for present action.
confusions.why_not: In the sheets the historical space is a memory-world traversed, not a situation to be acted on.

diff.counterfeit: A period costume drama set entirely in 1812 is simply set in the past; it has one chronological layer, not coexisting sheets.

confidence.high: One continuous space in which several historical periods meet or are passed through without transition logic (the Hermitage walk).
confidence.medium: Non-chronological memory jumps that are not tied to a clear present frame.
confidence.low: Any single shot of old décor.

diff.deamer_anchor: 'no cause and effect, just events that ricochet' (p.154)

examples.title: WarGames · S16 Falken's Pterodactyl, Dinosaurs & The Futility of Tic-Tac-Toe
examples.note: Cretaceous extinction (the pterodactyl slide), the 1973 death of Joshua, and the imminent 1983 nuclear strike coexist on Falken's face as layers of time.
examples.flip: the dinosaur is felt as a primal impulse rather than a coexisting sheet of the past

examples.title: WarGames · S08 Discovering 'Joshua'
examples.note: The microfiche frame layers Falken's family past directly into David's present search, two temporal strata visible in one glowing pane.
examples.flip: the image functions simply as a practical clue to guess the password

examples.title: WarGames · S17 Shoreline Despair, Helicopter Rescue & Race Against the Cheyenne Mountain Blast Doors
examples.note: Falken stands in the war room he designed a decade earlier, his past creation (Joshua) speaking back to him from the mainframes.
examples.query: S17 · Goose Island Shore / NORAD Blast Doors
