examples.title: WarGames · S08 Discovering 'Joshua'
examples.note: Reels of microfiche spin past headlines of Falken's career and obituary, traversing stacked sheets of archived time.
examples.flip: the microfiche pages must be read as text documents

signs.name: Powers of the false
signs.definition: The genetic chronosign, oriented toward the future: narration stops claiming to be true and works through series, repeating things with differences and letting fake and real bleed together, so truth has to be made rather than found.
signs.deamer_quote: ‘no longer concerned with a pretence to truth, but instead with exposing this pretence’ (p.155)
deleuze_examples: F for Fake (Orson Welles, 1973) - the art forger Elmyr and the faked Picassos
Touch of Evil (Orson Welles, 1958) - Quinlan's planted evidence
Moi, un noir (Jean Rouch, 1958) - Abidjan dockworkers acting out their own fabulations
Pour la suite du monde (Pierre Perrault / Michel Brault, 1963) - islanders restaging the beluga hunt
signs.deleuze_examples_source: Deamer's Section II (pp.138-172) cites no films for these signs; examples are Deleuze's own from Cinema 2, supplied from Cinema 2 rather than from Deamer.

scenes: Static long-take interviews with Factory 420's workers facing the camera, some real and some scripted and played by actors.
Former apprentice He Xing remembers master tooler Wang among the factory's machines.
Little Flower tells how she was named after a Joan Chen film, and is played by Joan Chen herself.
The factory is to be torn down and replaced by the luxury '24 City' apartment complex.

signs.operation: Film a sincere face-to-camera testimony, then give the same words to an actor, and never mark where the switch happens.
signs.shot_criteria: A shot that stages testimony, copying or fabrication: people speaking straight to camera in a work setting, forgery or imitation in action, demolition to make way for a replacement, or identical things repeated in series.
signs.gloss: serialism, the ongoing ungrounding of the image
signs.question: What if contradiction generates rather than obstructs the story?

diff.difference: Does the film expose its own claim to truth, with testimony, performance or versions that pass into one another so that no image can be held as the true one?
diff.axis: chronosign: which order of time organises narration; peaks of the present (coexisting presents) / sheets of the past (coexisting strata of past, non-chronological) / powers of the false (series of time: becoming that falsifies, genesis)

confusions.name: Limpid and opaque
confusions.flip: It is limpid and opaque instead if the exchange is local to one image (the glass, the role) and the narration's truth is not at stake.
confusions.why_not: The powers of the false act on the series of the narration, not on one image's two faces.

confusions.name: Theatrical figure
confusions.flip: It is a theatrical figure instead if the deception is a role inside a stable plot that is eventually unmasked.
confusions.why_not: The powers of the false have no unmasking: there is no underlying truth to reveal.

confusions.name: Demark
confusions.flip: It is a demark instead if one aberrant item breaks a logic that is then restored by thinking it through.
confusions.why_not: The powers of the false do not re-orient a logic; they make falsification itself the process.

diff.counterfeit: A twist ending that reveals the narrator lied reinstates a true version; that is a demark or reversal, not the powers of the false.

confidence.high: Actors and real witnesses are intermixed without markers, or one story is told in several incompatible versions none of which is privileged.
confidence.medium: An unreliable testimony device that is only partly resolved.
confidence.low: A single talking-head shot (which could be documentary, fiction or both).

diff.deamer_anchor: 'no longer concerned with a pretence to truth … exposing this pretence' (p.155)

signs.name: Bodies of attitude
signs.definition: The first noosign: an everyday body shown in its postures, tiredness and habits instead of in action or imitation. The body comes before the plot and breaks up into many incompatible ways of being present.
signs.deamer_quote: ‘Attitude describes a body that does not act, that is displayed in its complex everydayness’ (p.158)
deleuze_examples: Shadows (John Cassavetes, 1959) - bodies drifting through daily attitudes
Faces (John Cassavetes, 1968) - bodies worn down by waiting and fatigue
Jeanne Dielman, 23 quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles (Chantal Akerman, 1975) - the daily routines of a body in the kitchen
Sleep (Andy Warhol, 1963) - the body filmed in its most everyday posture
signs.deleuze_examples_source: Deamer's Section II (pp.138-172) cites no films for these signs; examples are Deleuze's own from Cinema 2, supplied from Cinema 2 rather than from Deamer.

scenes: An eleven-year-old Black boy calling himself Woody Guthrie hops freight trains with a guitar case reading 'This machine kills fascists'.
Jude Quinn (Cate Blanchett) plays electric guitar with a band and shocks the folk audience.
Billy McCarty lives quietly as an old outlaw in an Old West town.
Jack Rollins, a folk singer seen in a documentary, reappears as a gospel-singing minister, Father John.

signs.operation: Film the body between actions, waiting, slumping, fidgeting, and let several different bodies stand in for one person.
signs.shot_criteria: A body shown in posture rather than purposeful action (sleeping, waiting, yawning, idling, repeating a chore, drifting through a journey), with its tiredness or habits visible in the frame.
signs.gloss: a dispersed individuation of the body
signs.question: What does the body think before it acts?

diff.difference: Is the body shown waiting, tired, slumped or posing, in its everydayness, with the posture itself as the content and no act prepared or completed?
diff.axis: noosign: where thought appears; body of attitude (body at rest, dispersed in everydayness) / body of gest (attitudes linked into a performed social act) / cinema of the brain (the world or mise-en-scène as a brain, genesis)

confusions.name: Body of gest
confusions.flip: It is a body of gest instead if attitudes are linked into a performed social gesture addressed or staged (Brechtian demonstration, ritual, choreographed routine).
confusions.why_not: Attitude is the body before linkage; the gest strings attitudes into a social act.

confusions.name: Quotidian
confusions.flip: It is the quotidian instead if everyday life is framed as a critical figure inside a film still ruled by action.
confusions.why_not: In the body of attitude the everyday posture becomes the site of thought, not a comment within a plot.

confusions.name: Enfeeblement
confusions.flip: It is enfeeblement instead if the lassitude is the waning of a character's ability to act, measured against actions still expected.
confusions.why_not: The body of attitude is not failing to act; action is simply not its register.

diff.counterfeit: A soldier resting against a wall between battles is a pause in the action-image: the rest is recovery for the next act.

confidence.high: Long takes of bodies waiting, lying or posing with no narrative payoff, sustained across the film.
confidence.medium: A single sustained posture shot within a loose narrative.
confidence.low: A still of someone sitting (could be any of attitude, quotidian or enfeeblement).

diff.deamer_anchor: 'a body that does not act … displayed in its complex everydayness' (p.158)

examples.title: WarGames · S12 Inside WOPR, DEFCON 4 & 'Machines Don't Call People'
examples.note: David sits slumped on the infirmary bed with handcuffed wrists, his exhausted teenaged posture thinking through his predicament before any plan forms.
examples.query: S12 · NORAD Computer Floor & McKittrick's Office
examples.flip: the shot cuts in to his face as an affective close-up

examples.note: On the dark Goose Island shore, David and Jennifer sit huddled against the cold, their weary bodies registering the weight of an unwinnable deadline.
examples.flip: their posture is just an ordinary rest stop during the journey

examples.note: Captain Jerry leans heavily over the silo console on his elbows, his bodily hesitation preceding his spoken refusal to launch.

examples.note: Falken reclines in the shadows of his living room chair, his resigned posture embodying his philosophy of evolutionary surrender.
examples.flip: his spoken monologue carries the thought rather than his bodily attitude

signs.name: Bodies of gest
signs.definition: The second noosign: attitudes are tied together and theatricalised into a ceremony or social gesture (Brecht's gest), a collective statement of the body that can end with the visible body disappearing.
signs.deamer_quote: ‘The gest is that which links attitudes’ (p.159)
deleuze_examples: Le Lit de la vierge (Philippe Garrel, 1969) - bodies put through ceremony
Salome (Carmelo Bene, 1972) - the grotesque, theatricalised body
L'Amour fou (Jacques Rivette, 1969) - rehearsal turning bodies into theatre
Shadows (John Cassavetes, 1959) - gest as the link between attitudes
signs.deleuze_examples_source: Deamer's Section II (pp.138-172) cites no films for these signs; examples are Deleuze's own from Cinema 2, supplied from Cinema 2 rather than from Deamer.

scenes: Cristi, a plainclothes cop, follows the teenage student Alex through the town in long, uneventful takes of trailing and waiting.
At home Cristi eats his dinner while his wife plays the same Romanian pop song over and over, and they argue about what the words mean.
In Captain Anghelache's office the captain has a dictionary brought in and reads out 'conscience', 'law', 'police'.
The last shot frames only a whiteboard as the sting is drawn up; Cristi is no longer in the picture.

signs.operation: Take an everyday body into a ritual (an office, a uniform, a ceremony) and hold the frame until the ritual has swallowed the person.
signs.shot_criteria: Bodies turned into social ceremony or display in the frame: drill, uniforms, rituals, masks, mime, or official procedure (reading definitions, diagramming plans), with gesture shown as a public, repeated act.
signs.gloss: the linkage of attitudes creating differentiation
signs.question: How do postures become social relations?

diff.difference: Are postures chained into a visible, repeated or staged gesture that performs a social act (ritual, bureaucratic routine, demonstration) and is shown as performance, not as efficient action?
diff.axis: noosign: where thought appears; body of attitude (body at rest, dispersed in everydayness) / body of gest (attitudes linked into a performed social act) / cinema of the brain (the world or mise-en-scène as a brain, genesis)

confusions.name: Body of attitude
confusions.flip: It is a body of attitude instead if the body stays in one posture with no linkage into a performed act.
confusions.why_not: The gest links; the attitude rests.

confusions.name: Theatrical figure
confusions.flip: It is a theatrical figure instead if the performance is a character's disguise or play that serves a plot.
confusions.why_not: The gest is the social act of the body itself exhibited, not a mask worn for a narrative end.

confusions.name: Imprint
confusions.flip: It is an imprint instead if the gesture is the milieu's mark on the body, leading to action within the large form.
confusions.why_not: The gest does not convert into action on the world; it is exhibited as gesture.

diff.counterfeit: A cop's efficient arrest routine in a thriller is action; it becomes gest only if the film stages it as ritualised performance for us to examine.

confidence.high: Protracted, repeated social rituals (reading, filing, dictionary scenes, dances) shown at length as performance.
confidence.medium: One clearly staged gestural sequence.
confidence.low: A single frame of a gesture, which cannot show linkage.

diff.deamer_anchor: 'The gest is that which links attitudes' (p.159)

examples.title: WarGames · S02 McKittrick & Beringer Debate WOPR Taking Men Out of the Loop

signs.name: Cinema of the brain
signs.definition: The genetic noosign: thought appears in the mise-en-scene itself (sets, light, colour, sound) rather than in a character, and the world on screen becomes a map of the mind, a brain-screen.
signs.deamer_quote: ‘The screen becomes an image of the mind’ (p.160)
deleuze_examples: 2001: A Space Odyssey (Stanley Kubrick, 1968) - the Star Child and the cosmos as brain
The Shining (Stanley Kubrick, 1980) - the hotel and maze as a mental map
Je t'aime, je t'aime (Alain Resnais, 1968) - the brain-machine experiment
Mon oncle d'Amerique (Alain Resnais, 1980) - lab rats and Laborit's neurobiology
signs.deleuze_examples_source: Deamer's Section II (pp.138-172) cites no films for these signs; examples are Deleuze's own from Cinema 2, supplied from Cinema 2 rather than from Deamer.

scenes: A god's-eye shot of Elm Street, with streets and houses drawn in white chalk on a black sound stage and labelled by name.
Characters in Depression-era clothes walk among real furniture inside chalk-outline houses, with a dog drawn on the floor.
The surrounding world is pure black or pure white, switching between night and day in an instant.
Invisible doors creak and characters knock on walls that aren't there while a narrator's voice runs over everything.

signs.operation: Draw the town on the floor and shoot it from above, so the set works like a diagram of thought.
signs.shot_criteria: An environment presented as a map, model or diagram of thought (chalk or outline plans, overhead grids, mazes, anatomy/neural imagery, cosmic fields), where the place itself is the subject rather than a backdrop for action.
signs.gloss: the screen as a cerebral space
signs.question: Has the screen itself become a thinking system?

diff.difference: Is the set or world laid out as a map of thought (abstract floor plans, chalk-drawn spaces, landscapes as mental states), so that the screen reads as a brain rather than a place to act in?
diff.axis: noosign: where thought appears; body of attitude (body at rest, dispersed in everydayness) / body of gest (attitudes linked into a performed social act) / cinema of the brain (the world or mise-en-scène as a brain, genesis)

confusions.name: Seed and environment
confusions.flip: It is seed and environment instead if a miniature germ inside the world contains it, rather than the whole screen being the mental space.
confusions.why_not: The brain-cinema has no inner crystal; the whole field is cerebral.

confusions.name: Milieu
confusions.flip: It is a milieu instead if the environment determines characters' behaviour as a real situation to resolve.
confusions.why_not: The brain-screen's spaces do not determine action; they are thought itself topologised.

confusions.name: Gaseous perception
confusions.flip: It is gaseous perception instead if the image dissolves into acentred molecular movement (flicker, particles) without organising a mental map.
confusions.why_not: The cinema of the brain is highly organised; it is thought's architecture, not matter's dispersal.

diff.counterfeit: A stylised expressionist set in a horror film serves mood and action; it is décor for a plot, not the plot's brain.

confidence.high: The entire film uses an abstract or diagrammatic world (lines on a floor, recursive sets) that the narrative treats as literal.
confidence.medium: Sustained sequences of landscapes or architectures held as mental states.
confidence.low: A single stylised set shot.

diff.deamer_anchor: 'The screen becomes an image of the mind' (p.160)

signs.name: Lectosigns
signs.image_type: Lectosigns / the readable image (infinite of the time-image)
signs.definition: The limit of all time-images: once images stop linking up naturally, frame, shot, montage, colour and sound have to be read and relinked by the viewer, and the film only exists through interpretation.
signs.deamer_quote: ‘a film that not only demands to be seen, but requires a reading’ (p.163)
deleuze_examples: India Song (Marguerite Duras, 1975) - voices detached from the bodies on screen
Too Early, Too Late (Jean-Marie Straub / Daniele Huillet, 1982) - landscapes read as buried strata of history
Hitler: A Film from Germany (Hans-Jurgen Syberberg, 1977) - an image to be deciphered
Moses and Aaron (Straub / Huillet, 1975) - stratigraphic, readable image
signs.deleuze_examples_source: Deamer's Section II (pp.138-172) cites no films for these signs; examples are Deleuze's own from Cinema 2, supplied from Cinema 2 rather than from Deamer.

scenes: Oscar's DMT trip is six minutes of pulsating, morphing abstract smoke, fractal and kaleidoscope light.
From Oscar's point of view in the bathroom he splashes water on his face in the mirror; the shot comes back later reversed.
After death the camera floats overhead above the Tokyo night streets and neon, looking down.
In the coda, from the newborn's blurred point of view, a baby is born and presses into its mother's breast, then black.

signs.operation: Take away every link between shots and leave the viewer to read the sequence like a text.
signs.shot_criteria: An image that cannot be taken in at a glance and has to be deciphered: abstract light patterns, writing or text filling the frame, disorienting overhead or first-person views, or microscopic and organic forms that look like something else.
signs.gloss: the infinite of the time-image
signs.question: What must I read here that I cannot simply see?

diff.difference: Does grasping the film require you to relink its images, narration and narrative yourself, because none of them links 'naturally' and no single key object resolves it?
diff.axis: relation to the whole time-image: the lectosign is the common limit (∞) of all time-images, the reading that relinks hyalo-, chrono- and noosigns; the opposite pole from the zeroness (0) of opsign/sonsign; no triad

confusions.name: Symbol
confusions.flip: It is a symbol instead if an object hands the viewer a key that settles the meaning.
confusions.why_not: The lectosign offers no key; reading is relinking across the whole film.

confusions.name: Extreme limit
confusions.flip: It is the extreme limit instead if the difficulty is a proliferation of problems within a plot of action that the film itself poses and works through.
confusions.why_not: The lectosign's reading is not a problem the film sets and pursues; it opens onto what the film does not think.

confusions.name: Cinema of the brain
confusions.flip: It is (only) the cinema of the brain instead if one domain, the world as brain, carries the demand without frame, shot, montage, colour and sound all requiring reading.
confusions.why_not: The lectosign is the limit of all time-images together, not one noosign.

diff.counterfeit: A puzzle film with a final reveal requires attention but then reads itself for you; once the twist resolves it, it is a movement-image of thought, not a lectosign.

confidence.high: A whole film judged across frame, shot, montage, colour and sound, where every level refuses natural linkage.
confidence.medium: An extended sequence that demands relinking across several levels.
confidence.low: Any single shot.
